explanations: terra: Rain brings fruits from the earth as provision, a compact divine field scene in which the product is received rather than self-created.

luna: The section interprets tazkiya as a wealth share given to purify; this ayah defines righteousness through giving wealth to named recipients, prayer, and zakat, specifying the ethical acts behind that purification.
terra: One pilgrim asks only for worldly benefit and consequently has no share in the afterlife, closely matching the worldly tilth with no afterlife portion in 42:20.
terra: The contrasting prayer asks for good in both the world and the afterlife, refusing to make the nearer field the sole crop.
terra: Those who ask for both goods receive a share of what they have earned, joining labor, portion, and lasting outcome.

luna: The section contrasts tended ground and a field whose growth is lost; this ayah describes a corrupt person striving to destroy crops and offspring, making deliberate destruction the field's moral opposite. | terra: The corrupt person destroys cultivated land and progeny, reversing the Lord-like work of maintaining and repairing a farm.
terra: The answer to what should be spent is العفو, commonly understood as what can be spared; this may illuminate a measured share that leaves a sound remainder, though it is not a harvest rule.
terra: A good loan to God is multiplied many times, expressing the paid share as increase held beyond the immediate possession.

luna: The section's ز ك و includes growth and an apportioned gift; this ayah compares spending in God's way to a grain producing seven ears, making giving and multiplying harvest one image. | terra: Spending wealth is pictured as one grain producing seven ears and multiplied seed, joining gift, crop, and increase.
terra: Those who spend without reminders or injury retain their reward, specifying conduct by which a gift's fruit is not spoiled.
terra: A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, marking a boundary between cleansing gift and morally damaged gift.

luna: The section says the crop's given share cleans what remains; this ayah warns that reproach and harm can nullify charity, comparing such spending to soil washed from bare rock, a failed counterpart to fruitful giving. | terra: Charity spoiled by display and injury is like thin soil washed from rock by rain, a gift whose apparent field retains no yield.

luna: The section joins giving a share to blessed growth; this ayah pictures those who spend seeking God's approval as a garden on fertile ground that yields double after rain. | terra: Sincere spending is a high garden whose rain brings double yield, so giving itself becomes fruitful cultivation.
terra: A fruit garden is burned by a fiery whirlwind when its owner is most vulnerable, showing cultivated abundance without lasting security.

luna: The section names the root خ ر ج for what emerges and explains tazkiya as giving from produce; this ayah joins spending good things to what God brought forth from earth. | terra: Believers must spend from good earnings and from what God brings out of the earth, making the field's produce the substance of the gift.
terra: Concealed charity to the poor is called better and is said to remove evil deeds, directly pairing a paid share with cleansing.
terra: Whatever good is spent benefits the giver and will be repaid in full, explaining how released wealth is not finally lost.

luna: The section's root ز ك و includes growth and charity; this ayah contrasts God erasing usury with making charities grow, clarifying the difference between increase by taking and increase through giving. | terra: God effaces usury but makes charities grow, the sharpest non-field statement of increase through giving rather than grasping.

luna: The section connects giving zakat to success and what remains; this ayah pairs belief, prayer, and zakat with reward from the Lord and freedom from fear, linking the given share to enduring recompense.
terra: Cultivated land is listed among the alluring provisions of worldly life, making the field itself one object of the preference named in 87:16.
terra: What is better than those worldly attractions is then identified as abiding gardens with the Lord, turning cultivation toward its lasting end.
terra: Mary's Lord accepts her graciously and makes her grow with good growth, an explicit human counterpart to divinely blessed cultivation.
terra: One does not attain enduring goodness until giving from what one loves, specifying the costly share by which good is reached.

luna: The section links a crop's fate to whether its yield is rightly cultivated and shared; this ayah compares what wrongdoers spend to a freezing wind that strikes and destroys a people's harvest, showing spending that yields no good. | terra: Worldly spending by wrongdoers is like a freezing wind that destroys a crop, an anti-harvest opposite to charity that multiplies.
terra: The ban on multiplied usury ends with the call to fear God so that one may attain falah, opposing grasped increase to purified success.
terra: Those who withhold God's bounty mistake stinginess for good, but what they hoard becomes a burden, reversing the good remainder produced by giving.
terra: People who claim purity for themselves are corrected: God purifies whom He wills, a boundary on treating tazakka as self-produced growth.
terra: Worldly enjoyment is called little and the afterlife better for the God-fearing, tying the better field to the same fearing stance as 87:10.
terra: Prayer, zakat, and a good loan are followed by cleansing of evils and entry into rivered gardens, joining the share, purification, and lasting yield.
terra: Worldly life is play and diversion while the afterlife home is better for those who fear, another specific statement of the two valuations behind the field choice.
terra: God splits the grain and date-stone and brings living from dead, placing divine opening at the seed inside the section's split field.

luna: The section describes grain growing from split earth; this ayah stages rain producing green growth, grain, dates, grapes, olives, and pomegranates, making divine provision visible in harvest. | terra: Water produces vegetation, layered grain, and ripening fruit, and the reader is told to look at fruiting and maturity; this is the field's growth made visible.
terra: The idolaters assign invented portions of crops to God and partners, a precise corruption of the harvest's true due.

luna: The section says the purified share is the crop's due; this ayah commands giving the crop's حق on its harvest day, making the right part of the field's yield. | terra: Fruit-bearing gardens are followed by the command to give the produce's due on harvest day, exactly the section's grown crop and paid share.

luna: The section's field depends on growth after water; this ayah sends rain-bearing clouds to dead land and brings out fruits, connecting earth's revival to produce. | terra: Rain is carried to dead land and brings out every fruit, supplying the divine watering behind the good and bad soils compared in 7:58.

luna: The section contrasts a productive field with ground whose growth fails; this ayah says good soil yields plants by its Lord's leave while bad soil yields little, making soil and care visible in the difference of outcome. | terra: Good soil yields by its Lord's permission while bad soil yields only meager growth, a direct distinction between two outcomes on the earth.

luna: This ayah promises mercy to those who fear God, pay zakat, and believe; the next ayah calls its followers successful, making the section's link between a given share and success explicit across the passage.

luna: This ayah concludes that followers of the Messenger are successful; 7:156 immediately before it names paying zakat among the traits of those promised mercy, joining the image's given share to falah while each verse contributes a distinct part.

luna: The section's field is purified when its rightful share is paid; this ayah condemns hoarding gold and silver without spending in God's way, the opposite treatment of wealth. | terra: Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it are warned, a concrete reversal of wealth released in purification.
luna: This continuation describes the consequence of hoarding by using heated treasure to brand its possessors, completing 9:34's warning against withholding wealth's due.
terra: The addressees are asked whether they are content with worldly life instead of the afterlife and are told its enjoyment is slight.
luna: The section explains zakat as a share given from wealth; this ayah assigns the alms to the poor, needy, collectors, and other named recipients, specifying who may receive that share.
terra: Believing men and women support one another, establish prayer, and give zakat before the promised mercy and garden reward.
terra: Their promised gardens and enduring dwellings turn the preceding zakat into a lasting, fruitful destination and call that the great success.
terra: The Messenger and believers strive with wealth and lives, receive good things, and are called the successful; it is a distinct wealth-to-falah route.

luna: The section's root ز ك و includes charity and purification; this ayah pairs sadaqa from wealth with cleansing and growth, making the share itself both purifying and increasing. | terra: The charity taken from wealth both cleans and causes growth, expressed by تطهرهم وتزكيهم بها; it directly explains how the share purifies what remains.
terra: God is said to accept repentance and take charities, identifying the Lord as the ultimate receiver of the share released from wealth.

luna: The section says pasture can dry and be carried away; this ayah likens worldly life to rain-grown plants that become harvested down as if absent the day before, making apparent flourishing transient. | terra: Worldly life is a rain-grown field whose owners think it mastered, then God's command leaves it as mown as if it had never flourished.
terra: Those who desire worldly life and its adornment are paid their works in full here, a crop intentionally confined to the nearer field.
terra: For those worldly workers nothing remains in the afterlife but fire and their works become void, stating the failed permanence of that harvest.
terra: Full measure and weight and refusal to diminish people's goods explain the just dealing whose God-given remainder is called better in 11:86.
terra: بَقِيَّتُ ٱللَّهِ خَيْرٌ names the God-given remainder as better after honest dealing, closely matching the clean remainder of a paid due.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss for the remaining yield links success to what is preserved; Joseph tells the people to sow, harvest, and leave most grain in its ears, a measured reserve carried through future years. | terra: Joseph commands seven years of sowing and leaving the harvested grain in its ears except a little eaten, a concrete picture of yield and preserved remainder.

luna: The section contrasts a crop that is harvested and its due paid with vegetation lost; this ayah's coming drought consumes stored produce except a little kept, showing why measured remainder matters. | terra: Hard years consume the stored harvest except a little kept back, making the preserved remainder the field's means of survival.

luna: This ayah follows the years of stored grain with a year of rain and pressing produce; the sequence completes the section's account of crop output across measured seasons. | terra: A year of rain and pressing produce restores yield after famine, completing the managed crop cycle.
terra: The afterlife home is called better for those who fear, repeating the link between fear and the better lasting destination.

luna: The section contrasts neighboring ground with different fates; this ayah explicitly describes adjacent plots, watered alike yet differing in yield, so cultivation's outcome is not reducible to shared soil. | terra: Adjoining plots receive the same water yet differ in fruit, sharpening the section's contrast between fields sharing one ground.

luna: The section contrasts what the flood carries away with a productive yield that remains; this ayah's flood carries foam off while what benefits people stays on earth, clarifying the difference between passing residue and lasting use. | terra: Flood foam vanishes while what benefits people remains on earth, a parallel sorting of waste from the beneficial remainder.
terra: People rejoice in worldly life even though it is only a passing enjoyment beside the afterlife, distinguishing temporary provision from final gain.

luna: The section's roots connect growth to staying in good; this ayah compares a good word to a sound tree, giving the image a rooted form of enduring growth. | terra: A good word is a good tree with firm root and high branch, an organic image of goodness made stable.

luna: This continuation says the tree yields fruit every season by its Lord's leave, directly joining growth to recurring yield and divine care. | terra: That tree gives fruit every season by its Lord's permission, making persistence in good a recurring yield.

luna: The contrast is a bad tree uprooted from the earth with no stability, the opposite of the section's tended crop that grows and remains fruitful. | terra: A corrupt word is an uprooted bad tree with no stability, the plant-image opposite to growth that remains in good.
terra: God sends down water and brings out fruits as provision, assigning the field's useful yield to its Lord.
terra: God spreads the earth and causes every well-balanced thing to grow in it, joining cultivation to fitting measure.
terra: God places livelihoods on earth for people and for creatures they do not provide for, widening the beneficiaries of the measured growth in 15:19.
terra: God's treasuries release everything only in a known measure, closely matching the section's measured outgoing share and divine provision.
terra: Fertilizing winds and water from heaven are supplied while humans do not control its stores, locating crop growth in divine husbandry.

luna: The section's pasture is a crop that serves living creatures; this ayah gives rain to drink and trees in which livestock graze, supplying the water and fodder around the cultivated scene. | terra: God-sent water supplies drink and grows the vegetation in which livestock pasture, locating field and pasture under one provision.

luna: This continuation says rain grows crops, olives, dates, grapes, and fruits; it expands the section's field image into varied yield. | terra: The same water grows crops, olives, palms, grapes, and every fruit, a broad inventory of blessed cultivated growth.
terra: Those receptive to their Lord's revelation are promised good here and a better home in the afterlife, repeating the better destination of good action.

luna: The section's root ب ق ي names both harvest remainder and what endures; this ayah contrasts what people have that perishes with what is with God that remains. | terra: What people possess runs out while what is with God remains, stating the permanence within the section's definition of falah.
terra: Whoever wants the immediate life receives only what God chooses before reaching a destructive end, defining one deliberately short-term cultivation.
terra: Whoever seeks the afterlife with fitting effort and faith has that effort appreciated, the active counterpart to sowing for the afterlife.

luna: The section says a rightful portion is given from the yield; this ayah commands giving relatives, the needy, and travelers their due, making the harvest's share part of a broader obligation to distribute wealth. | terra: The command to give kin, the poor, and the traveler their due generalizes the harvest command's language of a right that must be paid.
terra: The prohibition on squandering immediately after giving each claimant his due prevents payment of the share from becoming waste.
terra: Full measure and just weight are commanded and called better in outcome, clarifying how a due is paid without corrupting the remainder.
terra: The parable's two vineyards, palms, and intervening crop form a fully cultivated estate rather than wild pasture.

luna: The section follows cultivated yield from growth to a harvest share; this ayah says the two gardens gave their produce without failing and had a river between them, staging productive abundance. | terra: Both gardens give their fruit without withholding anything, presenting complete yield before the owner's failure.
terra: Possession of abundant fruit leads the garden owner to boast in wealth and followers, exposing the worldly preference attached to the yield.

luna: The garden owner enters his productive garden while wronging himself; this ayah begins the contrast between a crop's visible abundance and the owner's false confidence that it will last. | terra: The owner enters his garden and claims it will never perish, mistaking a fruitful field for an inherently lasting possession.

luna: The owner says he does not think his garden will ever perish; this claim directly tests the section's distinction between temporary worldly yield and what truly remains. | terra: He doubts the Hour and assumes an even better return if restored to his Lord, carrying false confidence in the garden into the afterlife.
terra: The believing companion says entry into the garden should acknowledge God's will and power, naming the stance proper to received growth.

luna: The section contrasts fields that endure with growth that is lost; this ayah warns that the garden can be struck from heaven and left barren, reversing its earlier abundance. | terra: He warns that his Lord can give something better and send a calamity that leaves the garden barren and slippery.

luna: This continuation says the garden's water could sink into the earth beyond recovery, specifying another way its cultivated yield can fail. | terra: The garden's water may sink beyond recovery, exposing the hidden provision on which its growth depends.

luna: This ayah says the garden's fruits were destroyed and its owner wrung his hands; it completes the reversal from productive garden to lost yield, the opposite of harvest whose due is given. | terra: The fruit is encompassed and its owner wrings his hands over ruined trellises, a cultivated yield reduced to loss.
terra: After the garden's collapse, true protection belongs to God, who is better in reward and outcome; this identifies the lasting good the owner missed.

luna: The section contrasts cultivated growth with vegetation that dries and is swept off; this ayah says rain-grown plants become dry stubble scattered by winds, directly staging that fate. | terra: Worldly life is rain-grown vegetation that becomes dry fragments scattered by wind, directly aligning the nearer life with transient growth.

luna: The section joins a paid share to what lasts; this ayah calls wealth and children worldly adornment but says enduring righteous deeds are better in reward and hope. | terra: Worldly wealth is adornment, while enduring righteous deeds are better with the Lord in reward and hope, closely echoing خير and بقاء together.
terra: The people offer a kharj in exchange for protective work; this payment sense illuminates the section's named kharj/kharaj branch without itself being a crop due.
terra: After God increases the guided in guidance, enduring righteous deeds are better with the Lord in reward and return.

luna: The section's root ر ب ب is glossed as tending a farm; this ayah presents God making earth a dwelling, sending water, and bringing forth varied plants, framing the cultivated land as sustained provision. | terra: God makes the earth serviceable, sends water, and brings out diverse pairs of plants, echoing the One who tends and brings forth the field.

luna: The section connects growth to products for use; this continuation tells people to eat and pasture livestock, completing the plant scene with its human and animal yield. | terra: People are told to eat and pasture their livestock from that growth, specifying the crop's beneficiaries.
terra: The magicians say God is better and more enduring, the exact value pair that their later purification reward in 20:76 embodies.

luna: The section explains تَزَكَّىٰ through purification and giving; this ayah calls the gardens' reward for one who purifies himself, linking the field's inward work to lasting recompense. | terra: Gardens of lasting residence are named as the reward of the one who purifies himself, giving tazakka a garden and an enduring outcome.
terra: David and Solomon judge a crop damaged at night by sheep, a concrete boundary of responsibility around cultivated yield.

luna: The section makes ز ك و an image of growth; this ayah describes dead earth stirring, swelling, and producing varied growth after rain, a close parallel for emergence from soil. | terra: Barren earth stirs, swells, and grows every beautiful pair when rain falls, turning hidden life into visible increase.
terra: Rain makes the earth green under God's subtle care, a concise image of hidden provision becoming visible growth.

luna: The section's root ف ل ح has the success sense of remaining in good; this ayah uses أَفْلَحَ for the believers, giving the field's agricultural word its Quranic success sense. | terra: The declaration that the believers have attained falah supplies the result later specified by their performance of zakat.

luna: The section explains ز ك و as growth, charity, and purification; this ayah names those who perform zakat among the successful believers, joining the crop's given share to success. | terra: Within the portrait of those who attain falah, this ayah singles out those who actively perform zakat.
luna: The section links success to what remains in good; this continuation says the successful inherit Firdaws and abide there, specifying the lasting outcome of 23:1's success.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss of harvest yield includes a known measure; this ayah says water is sent down by measure, lodged in earth, and can be taken away, making provision measured and contingent. | terra: Water descends in measured amount and is lodged in the earth, while God can remove it; the field's source is both apportioned and precarious.

luna: After measured water, this ayah gives gardens of dates and grapes as food, a concrete result of the provision described in 23:18. | terra: That measured water produces palm and grape gardens with abundant fruit from which people eat.

luna: This continuation names the olive tree and its oil and condiment, extending the garden's produce into usable yield. | terra: The Sinai tree supplies oil and food, adding a useful harvested product to the gardens of 23:19.
terra: خَرَاجُ رَبِّكَ خَيْرٌ joins the section's named kharaj form to the Lord, what is better, and the One who provides.
terra: No one would become pure without God's grace and mercy, matching the dictionary claim that true growth comes from divine blessing.
terra: God sends pure water from heaven, placing purity itself at the source of the revival described in the next ayah.
terra: That water revives dead land and gives drink to animals and people, joining purification, growth, and provision.
terra: The faithful neither squander nor withhold when spending but keep a measured middle, a boundary around both the paid share and what remains.
terra: The question directs attention to how many noble plant-pairs God has grown from the earth, another command to read the ground's yield.
terra: The command to give full measure and not be among those who diminish restates the justice required when a known portion leaves one's goods.
terra: Straight weighing specifies the honest measurement by which the due is separated.
terra: People's goods must not be diminished and the earth must not be corrupted, extending just measurement into the care of the ground itself.
terra: God sends water and grows beautiful gardens whose trees humans could not grow, directly assigning the finished cultivation to Him.

luna: The section reads the field's successful remainder alongside 87:17's better and more abiding Hereafter; this ayah directly contrasts worldly provision with what is with God, which is better and more lasting. | terra: Worldly gifts are temporary adornment, whereas what is with God is better and more enduring.

luna: The section contrasts a worldly field with an afterlife field; this ayah says to seek the Hereafter with what God has given while not forgetting one's worldly share, making the two uses of provision explicit. | terra: God-given wealth is to seek the afterlife while retaining one's worldly share and avoiding corruption, a direct statement of how one provision is sown toward the lasting field.
terra: Worldly life is diversion while the afterlife is the true life, clarifying which field's growth counts as lasting life.

luna: The section describes purification through a property share; this ayah tells the hearer to give relatives, needy people, and travelers their حق, the due portion associated with material provision. | terra: Giving the relative, needy person, and traveler their right leads directly to the declaration that those givers are the successful.

luna: The section links ز ك و to growth and paying a share; this ayah contrasts wealth lent for increase with zakat given seeking God's face, whose givers are multiplied. | terra: Interest meant to increase wealth does not increase with God, whereas zakat given for His face makes its givers the multipliers.
luna: The section traces land from growth toward yield; this ayah asks the reader to look at the fruits of God's mercy as he revives the earth after its death.
terra: Those who perform zakat are also certain of the afterlife, combining the share with the field toward which it is sown.
terra: The people just described by zakat and afterlife certainty are declared the successful.
terra: Rain makes every noble kind grow on earth, assigning variety and increase to divine action.

luna: The section links pasture and crop to provision; this ayah describes water driven to barren land, crops grown for people and livestock, directly joining soil growth to use. | terra: Water is driven to barren land and brings out crops eaten by livestock and people, changing dead ground into provision.
terra: Saba's two gardens are a sign and provision from a good land under a forgiving Lord, a field explicitly held within gratitude.
terra: When the people of Saba turn away, their two fruitful gardens are replaced by bitter produce, tamarisk, and sparse lote trees.
terra: The replacement of the gardens is named recompense for ingratitude, defining the moral boundary exposed by their lost yield.
terra: God promises to replace whatever is spent, a non-agricultural statement of the share returning as provision rather than depletion.
terra: Whoever purifies himself does so for his own benefit, and the destination is God; this restates tazakka as a self-returning cultivation for the lasting end.
terra: Rain brings forth fruits of varied colors, another direct formulation of the Lord producing the field's yield.

luna: The section's field begins with growth from earth; this ayah calls dead earth a sign when revived and producing grain people eat. | terra: Dead earth is revived and grain is brought from it for people to eat, a compact field sequence of opening, growth, and benefit.

luna: This continuation adds date and grape gardens with springs to the grain scene, extending the field's growth into sustained fruit-bearing cultivation. | terra: Gardens of palms and grapes and flowing springs turn the revived soil into cultivated abundance.

luna: The continuation connects garden fruit to eating and provision; this completes the crop sequence with the yield that the section treats as a shareable product. | terra: People eat the gardens' fruit though their hands did not create it, pressing the distinction between farmer and divine Grower.

luna: The section traces growth toward a lasting good; this ayah shows crops grow, yellow, and become debris, a direct scene of what passes rather than remains. | terra: God waters varied crops, then they yellow and become debris; the complete cycle distinguishes visible growth from what lasts.

luna: The section connects success to lasting good; this ayah calls worldly life a passing enjoyment and the Hereafter the abode of permanence, defining what remains beyond the crop's season. | terra: The believing speaker calls worldly life brief enjoyment and the afterlife the settled home, a plain gloss on transient versus abiding gain.

luna: The section's crop depends on earth that can be made productive; this ayah describes humbled earth that revives and grows after water is sent down. | terra: Humbled earth stirs and swells when water falls, showing growth as revival by the One who gives life.

luna: The section's quoted ḥarth (tilth) divides seeking the Hereafter, whose field is increased, from seeking this world's field, which yields only a portion and no afterlife share; intention determines what kind of harvest endures. | terra: The afterlife is a tilth whose yield God increases, while worldly tilth gives no afterlife share; this states the section's two fields and two outcomes.
terra: Worldly provisions are temporary enjoyment, while what is with God is better and more enduring for trusting believers.

luna: The section moves from growth to a crop's measured yield; this ayah says God sends water in measure, revives dead land, and brings people forth likewise, joining measurement, soil, and growth. | terra: Water descends in a measured amount and revives dead land, linking measure, provision, and renewed growth.
terra: Provision descends from heaven and revives the earth after death, making the productive field one of the signs to be understood.
terra: Those called to spend who remain stingy only harm themselves, while God is rich; withheld produce therefore cannot secure its holder.

luna: The section relates crop growth to أَخْرَجَ and to 87:2's root س و ي for being set right; this ayah depicts a crop sending out its shoot, strengthening, thickening, and standing upright, a sustained growth rather than dried pasture. | terra: The community is a crop that sends out its shoot, strengthens, thickens, and stands on its stalk, a full picture of blessed growth that does not become chaff.

luna: The section develops measured growth into yield; this ayah pairs blessed rain with gardens and grain for harvest, showing the field's fruit as provision. | terra: Blessed rain grows gardens and harvest grain, bringing divine provision to the point of reaping.

luna: This continuation adds tall date palms with clustered fruit, another concrete yield from the water-grown landscape. | terra: Tall palms with layered clusters specify the mature produce of the rain-grown scene.

luna: The sequence names provision for servants and the reviving of dead land; it completes the crop scene by connecting field growth to sustenance. | terra: The harvest is provision for servants and revival for dead land, naming both beneficiary and source of renewed growth.

luna: The section's crop has a right that is paid; this ayah says a recognized حق in the believers' wealth belongs to the asker and deprived, specifying recipients for a share. | terra: A right for the asker and deprived person is located within the righteous person's wealth, matching the product's due rather than a voluntary leftover.
terra: The command not to declare oneself pure makes God's knowledge of the truly fearing person the measure of purification.
luna: The section treats cultivated ground as a source of yield; this ayah says earth is laid out for creatures, introducing a sequence of fruits, grain, and produce.
luna: The sequence names fruit and date palms with sheathed clusters, specifying the field's edible yield.
luna: This continuation names grain with husk and aromatic plants, extending the produce scene into grain and fodder.

luna: The section's root ب ق ي names what remains after yield and what endures; this ayah states that all on earth perishes, setting the contrast that the next ayah completes. | terra: Everything upon the earth is passing away, giving the cultivated world's produce its widest temporal boundary.

luna: This ayah says the face of the Lord remains; after 55:26's perishing earth, it gives a Quranic form of endurance beyond the section's passing crop and lasting Hereafter. | terra: The face of the majestic Lord remains after earthly things pass, identifying the only final permanence sought by the giver in 92:20.

luna: The section's field image turns success into tilling and growth; this ayah asks whether people have considered what they sow, placing their work beside God's control of the crop. | terra: The question about what people till stages the very act hidden in the section's agricultural sense of falah.

luna: The section's field scene moves from sowing to growth; this neighboring ayah says God is the one who makes the crop grow, completing the sowing question in 56:63. | terra: The next question assigns the crop's growth to God rather than the sower, matching growth received through divine blessing.

luna: The section contrasts a cultivated yield with pasture that dries and is swept away; this ayah says God could make what people cultivate into حطام, crop debris, the field's failed alternative. | terra: God could turn the crop into shattered dry matter, explicitly placing the tilled field under the pasture's chaff-like fate.

luna: After the crop could become debris in 56:65, this ayah gives the cultivators' imagined response that they would be burdened by loss; it sharpens the material cost of a ruined yield. | terra: The growers' stunned lament is the human response to the crop being turned into chaff and keeps 56:65 inside a farmer's experience.

luna: This neighboring ayah completes the crop-loss scenario with deprivation, contrasting the section's field whose due is paid from an actual yield. | terra: The ruined crop leaves the growers confessing that they are deprived, naming the lost share and remainder of a failed harvest.
terra: People are made successors over wealth and commanded to spend from it, fitting the field's Lord as true owner and the cultivator as steward.
terra: The good loan that God multiplies gives the share a promised return and generous reward.
terra: Men and women who give charity and lend God a good loan receive multiplied return, making gift the source of increase.

luna: The section contrasts durable success with pasture that withers; this ayah's rain-grown vegetation yellows and becomes chaff within its account of worldly life's brief display. | terra: The nearer life's growth delights the cultivators, then withers, yellows, and becomes debris before the ayah turns to the afterlife.

luna: The section links a property share to success; this ayah praises preferring others despite one's own need and says those guarded from stinginess are successful, giving the share a concrete ethical form. | terra: Those who prefer others despite their own need and are protected from avarice are called the successful, linking gift to falah.
terra: People are commanded to spend from provision before death makes them wish for time to give charity, placing a firm limit on when the share can bear fruit.

luna: The section connects a given share to falah; this ayah commands spending for one's own good and says those protected from the soul's stinginess are successful, linking release of wealth with success. | terra: The command to spend is joined to protection from the self's stinginess and then to falah, spelling out the moral work of the paid share.
terra: A good loan to God is multiplied and forgiven, continuing 64:16's spending-and-success sequence with increase and cleansing.

luna: The section's harvest image is a managed field and its yield; this neighboring story begins with owners of a garden planning to harvest it in the morning, supplying the setting for their later refusal of the poor. | terra: The tested garden owners swear to cut their fruit in the morning, beginning a harvest scene governed by their handling of its due.
terra: Their harvest oath allows no exception; the wording marks an absolute claim over a crop whose divine and human claims they ignore.
terra: A visitation from the Lord circles the garden while they sleep, reversing their assumed control over its yield.

luna: The section contrasts productive cultivation with growth that dries and is swept away; the garden owners wake to find their crop blackened, the reversal of a harvestable field. | terra: By morning the garden has become like a field already stripped or blackened, the withheld harvest made unavailable.

luna: The section explicitly speaks of the crop's right on harvest day; these garden owners set out early to cut its fruit, placing the harvest at the center of their plan. | terra: Their own summons to go early and cut the crop keeps the moral failure fixed on an actual harvest.

luna: The section says the crop's due is to be given; the garden owners instead resolve that no poor person should enter, a direct withholding of the yield's rightful share. | terra: The orchard owners resolve that no poor person will enter at harvest, directly reversing the command to give the crop's due.
terra: They approach confident that they can prevent access, making exclusion from the yield part of the planned harvest.

luna: After discovering their ruined garden, the owners recognize they were deprived; this completes the contrast between a rightly shared yield and a harvest lost after withholding its share. | terra: After withholding the poor person's share, the owners recognize that they themselves have been deprived of the yield.
terra: The most balanced owner asks why they did not glorify God, bringing the field failure into the stance commanded by سَبِّحْ.
terra: They finally glorify their Lord and confess wrongdoing, recognizing the true Master of the garden after its loss.
terra: Their admission of transgression identifies moral failure, rather than bad technique, as the cause illuminated by the ruined yield.
terra: They hope their Lord will replace the garden with a better one and turn back to Him, joining divine husbandry, loss, and better replacement.

luna: After the garden owners' refusal to admit the poor and the loss of their crop, this ayah says that worldly punishment is followed by greater punishment in the Hereafter, completing the consequence of withholding the harvest's share. | terra: The garden's earthly punishment is set beside the greater afterlife punishment, extending the harvest scene into the two destinies of 87:16-17.

luna: The section says the product's right is to be paid; this ayah describes a prescribed right in wealth, making the share a defined portion rather than whatever remains by chance. | terra: The worshippers' wealth contains a recognized due, a close counterpart to the known portion that must leave the harvest.

luna: This continuation identifies the prescribed right's recipients as the asker and deprived, completing 70:24's account of a due in wealth. | terra: The recognized due is assigned to the asker and the deprived, naming those for whom the share is held.
terra: God is said to have caused human beings to grow from the earth as a plant, extending the section's cultivated growth to the person who purifies himself.
terra: Prayer, zakat, and a good loan are followed by the promise that whatever good is sent ahead will be found with God better and greater in reward.
terra: People love the immediate life, naming the preference that makes worldly cultivation the chosen field.
terra: They leave the afterlife, completing the same choice between the two fields stated agriculturally in 42:20.

luna: The section's harvest due is a share that leaves the yield for others; this ayah shows the righteous giving food to the needy, orphan, and captive despite their own desire for it. | terra: The righteous give desired food to the poor, orphan, and captive, turning provision itself into the released share.

luna: The givers say they seek God's face and no repayment or thanks; this continuation specifies the intention behind 76:8's food-sharing, clarifying that the section's given share is not a transaction for return. | terra: They feed only for God's face and seek neither repayment nor thanks, matching the purified giver's motive in 92:20.
terra: Loving the immediate life and leaving a weighty day behind repeats the preference that makes temporary yield seem sufficient.

luna: The section's crop requires water for growth; this ayah sends abundant water from clouds as the opening of a sequence about grain and gardens. | terra: Abundant poured water begins a sequence that closely parallels 80:25-31.
luna: This continuation says the rain brings forth grain and plants, directly naming the field's products. | terra: God brings out grain and vegetation through that water, making the rain productive.

luna: The sequence ends in thick gardens, completing the growth from water through crop to cultivated abundance. | terra: Dense gardens complete the water, grain, and growth sequence as cultivated abundance.

luna: The section develops تَزَكَّىٰ as self-purification through growth and giving; Moses uses the same verb when he asks Pharaoh whether he will purify himself, offering another Quranic setting for the section's central action. | terra: Moses asks Pharaoh whether he will purify himself, turning tazakka into the direct invitation that precedes guidance and fear.
terra: Guidance to the Lord is meant to produce fear, joining the purification invitation to the receptive, fearing hearer of 87:10.
luna: The section rests on 87:4's أَخْرَجَ ٱلْمَرْعَىٰ and names the root خ ر ج; this ayah uses أَخْرَجَ for bringing out water and pasture, directly staging the same emergence of fodder.
luna: The section treats pasture and crop as sustenance whose yield matters; this ayah completes the preceding pasture scene by calling it provision for people and their livestock.
terra: Preferring worldly life is singled out as the decisive choice on the destructive side of the final outcome.
terra: Fearing the station of one's Lord and restraining desire gives the opposite stance, recalling the one who fears and accepts purification.
terra: The garden is the refuge for that fearing restraint, giving the successful choice a cultivated destination.
terra: The rebuked assumption that the blind man might purify himself directly connects reception of the message with tazakka.
terra: The alternative that he might take heed and benefit from the reminder connects that purification to the reminder of 87:9-10.

luna: The section makes a field's yield an object of reflection; this ayah opens the neighboring sequence by telling the human to look at food, whose production the next ayat stage. | terra: The command that a person look at his food opens the very field process the section asks the reader to see inside 87:14.

luna: The section frames purification through crop growth; this ayah's preceding rain poured abundantly supplies the water for the earth-splitting and food sequence that follows. | terra: Water is poured abundantly before the earth is split and planted, supplying the first action in the explicit field scene.

luna: The section's lexicon defines ف ل ح as splitting earth for tillage; this ayah says God splits the earth, the precise soil action that makes the field image visible. | terra: God's emphatic splitting of the earth is the Quran's literal counterpart to the section's ploughed, opened field.

luna: The section traces tilled soil into growing yield; this next ayah names grain as the first produce after the earth is split. | terra: After splitting the earth, God makes grain grow in it; the opened ground becomes productive rather than waste.

luna: The section develops the field's growing products; this ayah continues the food sequence with grapes. | terra: Grapes and herbage specify what the split earth produces in the continuing field scene begun in 80:25-27.

luna: The section develops the field's growing products; this ayah continues the food sequence with olives. | terra: Olives and date palms add cultivated, fruit-bearing plants to the yield of the opened earth.

luna: The section develops the field's growing products; this ayah continues the food sequence with date palms. | terra: Dense gardens show the split ground completed as tended and abundant cultivation.

luna: The section develops the field's produce and pasture; this ayah adds dense gardens to the sequence. | terra: Fruit and pasture distinguish human produce and grazing growth within the same divinely watered scene.

luna: The section ties field output to human use; this ayah completes the food sequence by calling the produce provision for people and their livestock. | terra: The whole yield is identified as provision for people and their livestock, stating the purpose of the productive field.
terra: Woe is declared for those who defraud in measure, the commercial opposite of giving the produce's rightful portion.
terra: The defrauders demand full measure when receiving from others, exposing grasping at the incoming share.
terra: When measuring or weighing for others they diminish it, directly reversing payment of the known due.
terra: The sky characterized by returning rain supplies the water paired with the split earth in the next ayah.
terra: The earth characterized by splitting, ٱلْأَرْضِ ذَاتِ ٱلصَّدْعِ, is a compressed parallel to water poured and ground opened for growth.

luna: The section connects أفلح to staying in good and تَزَكَّىٰ to purification and growth; this ayah joins success to the soul's purification, showing the field image's inner outcome. | terra: Success and purification meet in the same formula as 87:14, now with the soul as the thing cultivated.

luna: The section says growth can be suppressed like a seed buried in soil; this ayah's contrasting failure belongs to the one who دسّاها, burying or suppressing the soul, the inverse of cultivation. | terra: Burying or corrupting the soul ends in failure, the direct negative counterpart to successful purification and, in the section's field reading, to growth smothered underground.
terra: The successful sequence begins with one who gives and fears, uniting the paid share with the fearing hearer.
terra: Affirming the best outcome explains why the giver in 92:5 can treat what leaves his hand as seed for a better end.
terra: The giver who fears and affirms the best is promised ease, linking the share's path to the promise of ease in surah 87.
terra: The one who withholds and deems himself self-sufficient begins the exact reverse of the giver's purifying course.
terra: Denying the best outcome supplies the inward counterpart to withholding the share.
terra: The withholder is eased toward hardship, reversing both the giver's ease and the productive field's good end.
terra: The most God-fearing person is kept away from the fire before his wealth-giving purification is identified in 92:18.

luna: The section glosses تَزَكَّىٰ as giving charity from one's property; this ayah names the person who gives his wealth in order to purify himself, joining the same act to its inner aim. | terra: Giving one's wealth in order to purify oneself makes the paid share and tazakka one act.
terra: The giver is not repaying another person's favor, clarifying that the purifying gift is not an ordinary exchange for worldly return.
terra: The giver seeks only the face of his Lord, the Most High, joining purified giving to رَبِّكَ ٱلْأَعْلَى.
terra: The purified giver is promised satisfaction, completing the good end of the wealth that was released.
terra: The condemned person gathers wealth and repeatedly counts it, holding the whole yield rather than releasing its claim.
terra: He imagines that his wealth makes him permanent, the false worldly version of the section's abiding good.
